The location and configuration of the stations must consider ways to appropriately scale the facilities at major activity centers and intermodal hubs. Extensive simulation of ATN services in the 2000s revealed the criticality of anticipating surge flows at major intermodal stations and pre- positioning empty vehicles in anticipation of a scheduled fixed-route train to provide acceptable service and prevent “empty-vehicle starvation.” Such locations may benefit from co-locating vehicle storage to address the staging of empty vehicles to serve passenger demand surges as well as accommodating battery charging infrastructure. Further, these strategically placed storage areas for dormant vehicles also help accommodate the increase in the fleet size that is often necessary to service the periodic ridership surge-flow conditions that have been noted previously. Selected example cases—drawn from the referenced ATN system simulation modeling studies performed over the past 20 years—are discussed in subsequent editions of the report series, providing additional insight relevant to AMD implementation. 4.5 Systems Engineering Methodology for Analysis and Assessment NLR’s Phase III research concludes that there is a need for simulation-based analyses of AMD AV fleet operations considering the complexity of the integrated operating modes of on-demand and fixed-route transit services, corresponding station operations, need for battery charging and management of the fleet, and added complexity of roadway mixed-traffic operations—including the presence of pedestrians and other roadway users such as bicyclists. A methodology similar to, but expanding upon, the example simulation-based ATN studies will be described in detail in the next edition of this report series. The proposed multimodal simulations would be applied for analyzing the conceptual AMD network comprising multiple fleets of AVs operating in a geographically constrained environment, providing circulation service within the district and FMLM connections to regional transit, interregional transit, and parking facilities. This simulation methodology, referred to herein as SEM, would include all subsystems and modes and would stress test the system with hypothetical scenarios and edge cases to ensure the fleet, infrastructure, and operating methodology can adequately and safely serve demand in all situations.
